prosecution_strengths: Lifetime lookback for prior OWI offenses means decades-old convictions elevate current charges to felony level
Per se BAC threshold of .08 eliminates the need to prove actual impairment when chemical test results are available
defense_opportunities: Challenge the calibration records and maintenance logs of the Intoxilyzer device, as Wisconsin courts have suppressed results from improperly maintained instruments
Contest the legality of the traffic stop under the Fourth Amendment — Wisconsin requires reasonable suspicion, and field sobriety test administration errors can undermine probable cause
For drug OWI, challenge whether the restricted controlled substance was pharmacologically active at the time of driving, since THC metabolites persist in blood long after impairment ends
common_defenses: Improper stop — officer lacked reasonable suspicion for initial traffic stop
Rising blood alcohol defense — BAC was below .08 at time of driving but rose between the stop and the chemical test
Involuntary intoxication — medication interaction or unknowing consumption of alcohol
Challenge to field sobriety testing — non-standardized administration or medical conditions affecting performance

prosecution_strengths: Chemical test refusal under implied consent triggers automatic 12-month license revocation and may be used as evidence of consciousness of guilt
Even as a civil forfeiture, conviction triggers mandatory 6-9 month license revocation and alcohol assessment
defense_opportunities: Non-criminal civil forfeiture status means no jail time, no criminal record, and lower standard of proof arguments available
Challenge the 20-minute observation period required before breath testing — failure to observe is grounds for suppression
Negotiate for reduced charges such as inattentive driving or absolute sobriety violation to avoid OWI-related license consequences
common_defenses: Mouth alcohol contamination — recent use of mouthwash, GERD, or dental work affecting breath test accuracy
Improper observation period before chemical testing
Medical condition mimicking impairment (diabetes, neurological conditions)
Rising BAC — defendant was below .08 while actually operating the vehicle

prosecution_strengths: Wisconsin's lifetime lookback means any prior OWI from any state, at any time, counts toward the repeat offense level
Mandatory minimum incarceration increases sharply: 5 days (2nd), 45 days (3rd), 60 days (4th), 18 months (5th/6th)
Fourth offense is automatically a Class H Felony regardless of when prior offenses occurred
defense_opportunities: Challenge the validity of prior OWI convictions — if a prior was obtained without proper counsel or constitutional protections, it may not count for enhancement
Seek placement in the drug court or OWI treatment court program as an alternative to mandatory incarceration
Negotiate for extended supervision or electronic monitoring in lieu of a portion of mandatory jail time where statutes allow judicial discretion
Contest the accuracy of the prior offense record, particularly out-of-state convictions with incomplete documentation
common_defenses: Invalid prior convictions — prior plea taken without counsel or without understanding of rights
Constitutional challenge to the traffic stop or arrest procedure
Chemical test reliability — challenge instrument calibration, operator certification, or chain of custody
Necessity defense — driving was required to prevent greater harm

prosecution_strengths: Blood tests for restricted substances are highly sensitive and can detect presence well below pharmacologically active levels
Prosecution can rely on Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) protocol testimony to establish impairment beyond chemical test results
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether a detected substance was at a pharmacologically active level at the time of driving versus mere residual presence
Contest the DRE evaluation protocol — DRE conclusions are subjective and the 12-step protocol has documented error rates
For prescription medications, argue lawful use under valid prescription and that the substance was taken as directed
Challenge the blood draw procedure — improper venipuncture, contamination of sample, or lack of proper preservative in blood vial
common_defenses: Lawful prescription use — medication taken as directed by physician
No actual impairment — chemical presence alone does not prove impairment for non-per-se substances
Blood sample contamination or improper storage affecting test reliability
Involuntary intoxication — unknowing ingestion of controlled substance

prosecution_strengths: Broad statutory language ('endangered the safety of any person or property') gives prosecution wide latitude in charging
Dashcam, body cam, and surveillance footage frequently provide compelling evidence of driving behavior
Often paired with other charges (OWI, fleeing) creating cumulative sentencing exposure
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the driving behavior actually rose to 'wanton disregard for safety' versus mere negligence or carelessness
Negotiate reckless driving as a plea reduction from OWI to avoid OWI-specific consequences (license revocation, ignition interlock, insurance surcharges)
Present evidence of road conditions, mechanical failure, or emergency circumstances that explain the driving behavior
common_defenses: Emergency circumstances — defendant was responding to a genuine emergency
Mechanical failure — vehicle malfunction caused the erratic driving
Insufficient evidence — driving behavior did not rise to statutory 'wanton disregard' standard
Misidentification of the driver

prosecution_strengths: Surveillance camera networks and modern vehicle identification technology make identification of the vehicle highly likely
Consciousness of guilt inference from fleeing the scene is powerful before a jury
Hit-and-run involving death is a Class D Felony (up to 25 years), creating significant sentencing exposure
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the defendant had actual knowledge that an accident occurred — noise, road conditions, or vehicle size may prevent awareness
Present evidence that the defendant left the scene due to fear for personal safety and reported the accident shortly after
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant was unaware a collision occurred
Fear of harm — defendant left due to reasonable fear of violence at the scene and promptly reported the accident
Misidentification of the vehicle or driver
Duress — defendant fled under threat from passengers or others

prosecution_strengths: OWI homicide only requires proof that defendant was intoxicated and caused the death — no need to prove recklessness beyond the intoxication itself
Chemical test results establishing BAC above .08 combined with the fatal collision create a straightforward prosecution theory
Juries are typically sympathetic to victims in fatality cases, creating strong emotional weight
defense_opportunities: Challenge the causal link between intoxication and the fatal collision — argue that an independent intervening cause (other driver, road defect, mechanical failure) caused the death
Contest the BAC test results through chain of custody challenges, instrument reliability, or timing between accident and blood draw
Argue that the victim's own conduct (failure to wear seatbelt, their own impairment, traffic violations) was the proximate cause of death
common_defenses: Intervening cause — another driver's negligence or external factor caused the fatal collision
Challenge to causation — intoxication was not the proximate cause of death
Chemical test unreliability — blood draw timing, contamination, or instrument error
Victim's contributory conduct as proximate cause of the fatal injury

prosecution_strengths: Physical evidence at the crash scene (skid marks, vehicle data recorders, speed calculations) often establishes negligence clearly
Does not require proof of intoxication, making this easier to prove than OWI homicide
defense_opportunities: Distinguish between ordinary negligence (civil liability) and criminal negligence (criminal liability) — the conduct must be a gross deviation from the standard of care
Present evidence of sudden mechanical failure, unforeseeable road conditions, or medical emergency to negate criminal negligence
Negotiate from OWI homicide down to negligent homicide to avoid the 5-year mandatory minimum
common_defenses: Ordinary negligence versus criminal negligence — conduct did not rise to the criminal standard
Sudden emergency doctrine — unforeseeable circumstance caused the accident
Mechanical failure — vehicle defect was the actual cause
Victim's conduct contributed to or caused the fatal outcome

prosecution_strengths: DMV records provide straightforward documentary proof of suspension status
Notice of suspension sent by certified mail creates a presumption of knowledge under Wisconsin law
OWI-related suspensions carry enhanced penalties, creating additional sentencing leverage
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the defendant had actual knowledge of the suspension — mail delivery failures, address changes, or administrative errors in notification
Seek occupational license reinstatement as part of a resolution to reduce ongoing exposure
Argue that the underlying suspension was improperly imposed, which may invalidate the driving-on-suspended charge
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant never received notice of suspension
Invalid underlying suspension — administrative error in the suspension process
Necessity — driving was required for an emergency situation
Occupational license covered the driving at issue

prosecution_strengths: Fleeing is always a felony in Wisconsin (minimum Class I), creating serious exposure even for basic flight
Police dashcam and body cam footage typically provides clear evidence of the pursuit
If death results during the pursuit, the charge escalates to a Class F Felony (up to 12.5 years)
Prosecution can charge fleeing alongside the underlying offense, creating cumulative sentencing
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the officer's signal to stop was clearly visible or audible to the defendant — tinted windows, road noise, music may prevent perception
Argue the defendant was attempting to reach a safe, well-lit location before stopping rather than attempting to evade
Contest the 'knowingly' element — if defendant did not realize police were signaling them specifically
common_defenses: Lack of awareness — defendant did not see or hear the officer's signal to stop
Seeking a safe location — defendant was driving to a well-lit, populated area before stopping
Mistaken identity — officer pursued the wrong vehicle
Duress — defendant fled due to threats from passengers

prosecution_strengths: Physical possession or constructive possession (drugs found in defendant's vehicle, home, or personal effects) is often supported by strong physical evidence
defense_opportunities: First-offense simple possession is a misdemeanor — drug court and deferred prosecution programs may result in dismissal upon completion
Challenge constructive possession — proximity to contraband alone does not establish knowing possession, especially in shared spaces
Contest the legality of the search that produced the drugs — Fourth Amendment violations require suppression of evidence
common_defenses: Illegal search and seizure — drugs obtained through warrantless search without valid exception
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the substance was present or was a controlled substance
Lack of possession — drugs belonged to another person in a shared space
Entrapment — law enforcement induced the defendant to possess drugs they would not otherwise have possessed

prosecution_strengths: Wisconsin has not legalized recreational or medical marijuana, so any amount is criminal
Second THC possession offense is automatically a Class I Felony (up to 3.5 years)
Field testing kits provide rapid presumptive identification, giving officers probable cause for arrest
defense_opportunities: First-offense THC possession is a misdemeanor with a maximum of 6 months — diversion and deferred prosecution are commonly available
Some Wisconsin municipalities (Milwaukee, Madison) have local ordinances with lesser penalties for small amounts, potentially providing alternative charging
Challenge the substance identification — field test kits produce false positives, and lab confirmation may show a different substance or hemp (legal CBD)
common_defenses: Legal hemp — substance was CBD/hemp product with THC below the legal threshold
Illegal search and seizure — odor of marijuana alone may be insufficient for a warrantless vehicle search in evolving case law
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the substance contained THC
Misidentification of the substance by field test

prosecution_strengths: Cocaine as a Schedule II substance carries higher baseline penalties than marijuana possession
Laboratory confirmation of cocaine is highly reliable and difficult to challenge on scientific grounds
Second offense automatically becomes a Class I Felony
defense_opportunities: Challenge the search that produced the cocaine — consent searches, vehicle searches, and stop-and-frisk encounters each have constitutional requirements
Contest constructive possession when cocaine was found in a shared vehicle or residence
First-offense possession is still a misdemeanor — seek deferred prosecution or drug court diversion
common_defenses: Illegal search and seizure — the search violated the Fourth Amendment
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know cocaine was present
Constructive possession challenge — insufficient nexus between defendant and the contraband
Entrapment by law enforcement

prosecution_strengths: Methamphetamine is a Schedule II substance carrying significant penalties even for simple possession
Presence of meth paraphernalia (pipes, residue) provides corroborating evidence of knowing possession
Second offense is automatically a Class I Felony
defense_opportunities: Challenge the search and seizure — meth cases frequently arise from traffic stops with contested probable cause
First-offense possession remains a misdemeanor — drug treatment court may be available as an alternative to conviction
Contest the weight of the substance — trace or residual amounts may support a lesser charge or paraphernalia offense instead
common_defenses: Illegal search and seizure — warrantless search without valid exception
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the substance was methamphetamine
Constructive possession — insufficient evidence linking defendant to the substance in a shared space
Unwitting possession — substance was planted or left by another person

prosecution_strengths: Wisconsin's weight-based penalty tiers create escalating felony exposure: Class F (1-5g), Class E (5-15g), Class D (15-40g), Class C (40g+) for cocaine/heroin/meth
Mandatory minimums of 3-10 years apply at higher weight thresholds, limiting judicial discretion
Wiretap and surveillance evidence in trafficking investigations is typically extensive and difficult to challenge
defense_opportunities: Challenge the drug weight calculations — prosecution must prove the actual weight of the controlled substance, not the total mixture weight, for certain penalty thresholds
Contest the school zone measurement — the 1,000-foot zone must be measured correctly, and errors in measurement can eliminate the enhancement
Argue the defendant's role was minimal (courier, user-dealer) to seek lower sentencing within the guideline range
Challenge the reliability of confidential informant testimony — informants often have motives to exaggerate or fabricate
common_defenses: Illegal search and seizure — suppression of evidence obtained through constitutional violations
Entrapment — government agent induced the defendant to engage in trafficking they would not otherwise have pursued
Insufficient evidence of intent to deliver — possession was for personal use, not distribution
Challenge to confidential informant reliability and credibility

prosecution_strengths: Delivery of non-narcotic Schedule I-IV substances is a Class H Felony (up to 6 years), still carrying significant prison time
Controlled buys with audio/video recording provide strong direct evidence of delivery
THC (marijuana) delivery over 10,000g is a Class F Felony with substantial sentencing exposure
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'delivery' element — sharing or joint possession may not constitute delivery under Wisconsin law
Contest the identification of the substance — field tests are presumptive only, and lab analysis may show a different substance or concentration
Negotiate reduction from delivery to simple possession where the evidence of distribution is circumstantial
common_defenses: Accommodation — defendant shared drugs with a friend rather than commercially distributing
Entrapment — law enforcement induced the delivery
Illegal search and seizure — evidence should be suppressed
Misidentification of the substance

prosecution_strengths: Physical evidence from a clandestine lab (chemicals, equipment, residue) is typically overwhelming
Additional charges for child endangerment, environmental contamination, and cleanup costs compound exposure
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the defendant's activity constituted 'manufacturing' versus mere possession of precursor chemicals
Contest the defendant's knowledge of and participation in the manufacturing operation, especially in shared residences
Argue that the lab was not operational or that the defendant was merely present, not actively manufacturing
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know manufacturing was occurring on the premises
Mere presence — being present at a lab location does not establish participation in manufacturing
Illegal search and seizure — entry into the premises violated the Fourth Amendment
Insufficient evidence that the defendant performed any manufacturing act

prosecution_strengths: Paraphernalia is broadly defined and includes common household items when accompanied by drug residue or context
Often charged alongside possession of the underlying controlled substance to create cumulative penalties
defense_opportunities: Paraphernalia possession is a misdemeanor with only 30 days maximum — often the lowest-priority charge in a drug case
Challenge the 'knowing' element — argue the item had a legitimate, non-drug-related purpose
Negotiate dismissal of paraphernalia charge as part of a plea resolution on more serious co-charged offenses
common_defenses: Legitimate purpose — the item is a common household object with lawful uses
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the item contained drug residue or was associated with drug use
Illegal search — the paraphernalia was found through an unconstitutional search
The item does not meet the statutory definition of drug paraphernalia

prosecution_strengths: Intent to deliver is proven through circumstantial evidence: quantity, packaging, scales, large cash, multiple phones, and distribution paraphernalia
Penalties mirror delivery statutes, so possession with intent carries the same serious exposure as actual distribution
School zone enhancement doubles the sentence and applies broadly in Wisconsin
defense_opportunities: Challenge the inference of intent — argue the quantity, cash, or packaging is consistent with personal use rather than distribution
Contest the school zone measurement or applicability of the enhancement
Negotiate a reduction to simple possession if the evidence of intent is primarily circumstantial
common_defenses: Personal use — the quantity and packaging are consistent with personal consumption, not distribution
Illegal search and seizure — suppression of the evidence underlying the intent inference
Insufficient evidence of intent — cash and packaging have innocent explanations
Constructive possession — defendant did not have dominion and control over the drugs

prosecution_strengths: First-degree intentional homicide is Wisconsin's only Class A Felony — mandatory life sentence with minimum 20 years before extended supervision eligibility
Prosecution only needs to prove intent to kill plus causation — no requirement to prove motive
Wisconsin does not have the death penalty, which may make juries less hesitant to convict than in capital jurisdictions
Court can deny extended supervision eligibility entirely, imposing life without parole
defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent element — reckless conduct may support reckless homicide charges rather than intentional homicide
Contest forensic evidence (DNA, ballistics, blood spatter) through expert testimony
common_defenses: Self-defense — reasonable belief that deadly force was necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm
Defense of others — protecting a third person from imminent harm
Adequate provocation — heat of passion reducing the charge to a Class B Felony
Insanity or mental disease/defect — defendant lacked the capacity to form intent to kill
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who committed the killing

prosecution_strengths: The 'utter disregard for human life' standard, while higher than ordinary recklessness, is still a conduct-based standard rather than intent-based
Prosecution can present the reckless homicide theory as an alternative to intentional homicide, giving the jury multiple conviction options
defense_opportunities: Distinguish between ordinary recklessness (second-degree reckless homicide, Class D Felony, max 25 years) and 'utter disregard' (first-degree, Class B Felony, max 60 years)
Contest whether the defendant's conduct actually demonstrated 'utter disregard for human life' versus ordinary recklessness
common_defenses: Ordinary recklessness — conduct did not rise to 'utter disregard for human life,' supporting a lesser charge
Self-defense — defendant's reckless conduct was in response to an imminent threat
Accident — the death resulted from an unforeseeable accident, not criminal recklessness
Misidentification of the defendant

prosecution_strengths: Even mitigated to Class B Felony, the maximum penalty is 60 years imprisonment
Prosecution can argue provocation was not 'adequate' under the law, keeping the charge at first-degree intentional homicide
The prosecution can challenge the cooling-off period — if sufficient time passed for passion to subside, provocation fails
defense_opportunities: Adequate provocation mitigates from Class A Felony (life) to Class B Felony (60 years), providing a massive sentencing reduction
Present evidence of the provocative conduct and the defendant's emotional state to support the heat-of-passion element
Wisconsin's provocation framework is an affirmative defense that the defense raises, allowing strategic presentation to the jury
common_defenses: Heat of passion — killing occurred in the heat of passion after adequate provocation
Self-defense — partial self-defense may support a manslaughter verdict
Imperfect self-defense — defendant honestly but unreasonably believed deadly force was necessary
Mental health evidence supporting diminished capacity

prosecution_strengths: Criminal recklessness standard is lower than 'utter disregard' — ordinary recklessness is sufficient
Dangerous weapon enhancer adds 5 additional years
defense_opportunities: Distinguish between criminal recklessness and ordinary negligence — negligent conduct does not support a criminal conviction
Present evidence of unforeseeable circumstances that contributed to the death beyond the defendant's control
common_defenses: Ordinary negligence — defendant's conduct was careless but not criminally reckless
Accident — the death resulted from an unforeseeable event
Intervening cause — an independent event or the victim's own conduct caused the death
Lawful activity — defendant was engaged in a lawful activity that unexpectedly resulted in death

prosecution_strengths: Medical records documenting 'great bodily harm' (fractures, risk of death, permanent disfigurement) provide objective evidence
The intent element can be inferred from the severity of the attack
defense_opportunities: Challenge the classification of the injury as 'great bodily harm' versus 'substantial bodily harm' (Class I Felony, max 3.5 years) or 'bodily harm' (Class A Misdemeanor)
Contest the intent element — argue the harm was accidental or unintended during a mutual altercation
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant used reasonable force in response to an attack
Defense of others — defendant was protecting a third person
Lack of intent — the injury was accidental, not intentional
Mutual combat — both parties were willing participants in a physical altercation
Misidentification of the assailant

prosecution_strengths: Class A Misdemeanor is the most serious misdemeanor in Wisconsin, carrying up to 9 months and $10,000 fine
'Bodily harm' is broadly defined as physical pain or injury, illness, or impairment of physical condition — even minor pain qualifies
Victim testimony alone may be sufficient to establish the elements
defense_opportunities: Negotiate for a lesser charge such as disorderly conduct (Class B Misdemeanor, max 90 days) which avoids assault-specific collateral consequences
Challenge the victim's credibility, particularly in cases arising from interpersonal disputes
Argue that the contact was de minimis and did not actually cause bodily harm
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant acted to protect themselves from an aggressor
Consent — the physical contact occurred during a consensual activity
No bodily harm — the contact did not cause pain, injury, or impairment
Misidentification of the assailant

prosecution_strengths: Medical records objectively document the level of injury
Dangerous weapon enhancer adds 5 additional years
defense_opportunities: Challenge the injury classification — argue the injury does not meet the 'substantial bodily harm' threshold and should be charged as simple battery (misdemeanor)
Present self-defense arguments where the defendant was provoked or attacked first
Negotiate a plea to simple battery (Class A Misdemeanor) to avoid a felony conviction
common_defenses: Self-defense — reasonable response to an attack
Consent — contact occurred during a consensual activity (sports, mutual combat)
Accident — the injury was unintentional
Injury does not meet the substantial bodily harm threshold

prosecution_strengths: Class E Felony carrying up to 15 years, even without a weapon
Force or threat of force is a low threshold — snatching property forcibly from a person's hand qualifies
Victim identification testimony combined with physical evidence (surveillance, recovered property) is often compelling
defense_opportunities: Distinguish between robbery (force against person) and theft (no force) — if the taking did not involve force or threat, the robbery charge fails
Challenge the identification of the defendant through alibi evidence or witness reliability issues
Negotiate a reduction to theft charges where the force element is weak
common_defenses: No force or threat — the taking was a theft, not a robbery
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who committed the robbery
Alibi — defendant was elsewhere when the robbery occurred
Claim of right — defendant believed they had a legal right to the property

prosecution_strengths: Class C Felony carrying up to 40 years imprisonment — one of the most serious property crimes
Any article used or fashioned as a weapon qualifies, including replicas or simulated weapons
defense_opportunities: Challenge the identification of the defendant — armed robbery cases often involve disguised perpetrators
Contest whether the object was actually a 'dangerous weapon' under Wisconsin law
If the weapon was a replica or simulated, argue for a reduction to unarmed robbery (Class E Felony)
common_defenses: Misidentification — defendant was not the perpetrator
No weapon — object did not qualify as a dangerous weapon under the statute
Duress — defendant was forced to participate under threat of harm
Alibi — defendant was elsewhere at the time

prosecution_strengths: Class C Felony (40 years) for basic kidnapping; Class B Felony (60 years) if bodily harm or ransom involved
Broad statutory language covers any carrying away by force or threat of force without consent
Additional charges for sexual assault, robbery, or other crimes committed during the kidnapping compound exposure
defense_opportunities: Argue the movement was incidental to another offense (robbery, assault) and does not constitute a separate kidnapping under Wisconsin law
Challenge the 'without consent' element in domestic or custodial situations
Contest the use of force or threat — voluntary accompaniment is not kidnapping
common_defenses: Consent — the alleged victim went voluntarily
Incidental movement — the movement was inherent to another offense and does not support separate kidnapping charges
Parental rights — in custody disputes, the parent had lawful authority
Misidentification of the defendant

prosecution_strengths: Arson of a building is a Class C Felony (up to 40 years), regardless of whether it is a dwelling
Fire investigation evidence (accelerant detection, origin and cause analysis) is highly technical and often persuasive
Insurance fraud motive can be established through financial records, providing powerful circumstantial evidence
defense_opportunities: Challenge the fire investigation methodology — the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA 921) standards are complex and investigators sometimes misapply them
Contest the origin and cause determination — accidental fire causes (electrical, mechanical) are common and may explain the fire
If the defendant owned the property and no one was endangered, negotiate for lesser property damage charges
common_defenses: Accidental cause — the fire started from an accidental source, not intentional act
Lack of intent — defendant did not intend to damage the building by fire
Faulty fire investigation — methodology did not follow NFPA 921 standards
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who set the fire

prosecution_strengths: Class B Felony carrying up to 60 years — the same class as first-degree reckless homicide
Intent to kill can be inferred from the nature and severity of the attack (weapon used, location of injuries, statements)
Dangerous weapon enhancer adds 5 additional years
defense_opportunities: Challenge the specific intent to kill — argue the defendant intended to harm but not to kill, which may support a lesser assault charge
Self-defense — the defendant's actions were a reasonable response to an imminent threat
Argue voluntary abandonment — defendant ceased the attack before completion, which may mitigate the attempt charge
common_defenses: Lack of intent to kill — defendant did not have specific intent to cause death
Self-defense — defendant acted to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm
Voluntary abandonment — defendant voluntarily stopped the attack
Insufficient evidence — prosecution cannot prove acts 'demonstrating unequivocal intent to kill'

prosecution_strengths: Battery with a dangerous weapon enhancer adds 5 years to the underlying battery charge
Physical evidence of the weapon combined with injury evidence creates a strong prosecution case
defense_opportunities: Wisconsin does not have a standalone 'assault with a deadly weapon' statute — challenge whether the charges are properly structured
Self-defense — the weapon was used defensively in response to an attack
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant used the weapon to defend against an attacker
Accidental discharge or use — the weapon was not used intentionally
Not a dangerous weapon — the object does not meet the statutory definition
Misidentification of the assailant

prosecution_strengths: Wisconsin's tiered theft system creates felony exposure starting at $2,500, with escalating penalties up to Class F Felony for $100,000+
Theft from the person is always a Class G Felony regardless of value
Surveillance footage, transaction records, and recovered property provide strong evidence
defense_opportunities: Challenge the valuation of the property — the felony threshold ($2,500) determination can be contested with evidence of fair market value rather than replacement cost
Argue lack of intent to permanently deprive — temporary use or borrowing is not theft
Negotiate restitution and diversion for first-time offenders to avoid a conviction
common_defenses: Claim of right — defendant had a good-faith belief they had a right to the property
Lack of intent to permanently deprive — defendant intended to return the property
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who took the property
Consent — the owner authorized the taking

prosecution_strengths: Felony theft thresholds escalate: Class I ($2,500-$5,000), Class H ($5,000-$10,000), Class G ($10,000-$100,000), Class F ($100,000+)
Financial records, inventory systems, and forensic accounting provide clear evidence of loss amounts
Restitution is typically mandatory and can be a substantial financial burden
defense_opportunities: Contest the value calculation — push the amount below a felony threshold boundary to reduce the charge class
Challenge the evidence linking the defendant to the theft in cases involving multiple potential suspects
Negotiate a plea to a lower theft tier or deferred prosecution with full restitution
common_defenses: Valuation dispute — the property's fair market value is below the charged felony threshold
Claim of right — good-faith belief in ownership or entitlement
Insufficient evidence — cannot prove defendant took the property
Consent — defendant had permission from someone with apparent authority

prosecution_strengths: Class A Misdemeanor carrying up to 9 months and $10,000 fine
Surveillance evidence from retail establishments and public spaces is often clear
Repeat offenders face enhanced prosecution scrutiny
defense_opportunities: Misdemeanor status allows for deferred prosecution, diversion programs, and community service alternatives
Negotiate for a lesser charge (disorderly conduct) or municipal ordinance violation to avoid theft-specific consequences
First-time offenders often qualify for dismissal upon completion of a pretrial program
common_defenses: Lack of intent — defendant forgot to pay or made an honest mistake
Claim of right — defendant believed the property was theirs
De minimis — the value is trivial and prosecution is disproportionate
Misidentification

prosecution_strengths: Loss prevention officers and surveillance systems provide strong identification evidence
Civil recovery available to retailers creates additional financial pressure on defendants
defense_opportunities: Challenge the value of merchandise — push below the $500 felony threshold to keep charges at Class A Misdemeanor
Argue that the defendant did not pass the last point of sale, which may undermine proof of intent
Negotiate for a deferred prosecution or municipal citation for first-time offenders
common_defenses: Lack of intent — absent-mindedness, distraction, or confusion about payment
No concealment — defendant had merchandise in plain view and intended to pay
Misidentification — loss prevention identified the wrong person
Item was already purchased or belonged to the defendant

prosecution_strengths: Class F Felony (up to 12.5 years) for basic burglary — no requirement of nighttime entry or dwelling
Armed burglary or burglary with battery elevates to Class E Felony (up to 15 years)
Physical evidence (tool marks, fingerprints, DNA, surveillance) frequently links defendants to the entry
defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent element — entry without intent to commit a felony inside is criminal trespass, not burglary
Contest the 'without consent' element if the defendant had permission or believed they had permission to enter
Negotiate for criminal trespass (Class A Misdemeanor) or criminal damage to property where intent to commit an interior felony is not clearly established
common_defenses: No intent to commit a felony — defendant entered without criminal purpose
Consent or authority to enter — defendant had permission to be in the building
Misidentification — defendant was not the person who entered the building
Alibi — defendant was elsewhere at the time of the entry

prosecution_strengths: Same statute as commercial burglary but sentencing is typically more severe for dwelling entries
Armed or battery enhancement elevates to Class E Felony (15 years)
Victim impact from home invasion creates strong jury sympathy
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether the structure qualifies as a 'dwelling' under the statute
Argue the defendant had authority or invitation to enter, negating the 'without consent' element
common_defenses: Authority to enter — defendant had a key, invitation, or other authorization
No intent to commit felony inside — entry was for a lawful purpose
Misidentification — wrong suspect identified
Voluntary abandonment — defendant left before committing any interior offense

prosecution_strengths: Operating vehicle without owner's consent is a Class H Felony (up to 6 years) for the driver
Even passengers who know the vehicle is stolen face Class I Felony charges (up to 3.5 years)
GPS tracking, license plate readers, and surveillance cameras frequently identify the vehicle quickly
defense_opportunities: If the vehicle was abandoned undamaged, the charge may be reduced to a Class A Misdemeanor
Argue the defendant had a good-faith belief they had consent to use the vehicle from the owner or someone with apparent authority
Contest the 'without consent' element in cases involving shared vehicles, family members, or employer vehicles
common_defenses: Consent — defendant believed they had permission to use the vehicle
Claim of right — defendant had a good-faith ownership claim
Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the vehicle was stolen (passenger charges)
Misidentification of the driver

prosecution_strengths: Penalties mirror theft value tiers, so receiving high-value stolen property carries felony exposure
Knowledge that property was stolen can be inferred from circumstances: below-market price, no receipt, seller's reputation, altered serial numbers
Physical possession of stolen property shifts the evidentiary burden as a practical matter
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'knowing' element — defendant must have actually known the property was stolen, not merely been negligent
Contest the value of the property to push below felony thresholds
Argue the defendant acquired the property in good faith through a legitimate transaction
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know or have reason to believe the property was stolen
Good faith purchase — defendant bought the property at a reasonable price through a normal transaction
Claim of right — defendant believed the property was theirs
Property was not actually stolen

prosecution_strengths: Felony threshold is $2,500 in damages, covering significant property damage
Damage to religious or educational property is automatically a Class I Felony regardless of the amount
Restitution is mandatory and frequently substantial

prosecution_strengths: Posted signs or fencing create constructive notice, eliminating the need to prove actual verbal warning

prosecution_strengths: Evidence of intentional damage is often captured on surveillance or supported by witness testimony

Seek a civil compromise with the property owner as a basis for dismissal

Consent of the property owner
Misidentification of the defendant
De minimis damage — the amount does not justify prosecution

prosecution_strengths: 72-hour no-contact period is automatic and violation creates additional charges

False allegation — accusation made for strategic advantage in custody or divorce proceedings
Lack of bodily harm — the contact did not cause physical pain or injury

Present evidence of the victim's own aggressive conduct leading to the altercation
common_defenses: Self-defense — defendant used reasonable force to defend against the other party
Injury does not meet substantial bodily harm threshold — should be simple battery
False allegation — motivated by custody dispute, divorce, or revenge
Accident — the injury was unintentional during a mutual struggle

prosecution_strengths: If death results, the charge escalates to Class F Felony (up to 12.5 years); bodily harm to Class H Felony (up to 6 years)

No actual danger — the child was not placed in risk of harm under the circumstances

prosecution_strengths: Intentional great bodily harm to a child is a Class F Felony (up to 12.5 years); reckless great bodily harm is a Class H Felony (up to 6 years)

common_defenses: Accidental injury — the child's injury resulted from a fall, play, or other non-abusive cause

prosecution_strengths: The protective order itself is a court document with clear, specific terms that establish what conduct is prohibited

Contest the validity of the underlying protective order if it was issued without proper notice or hearing

Invalid underlying order — order was issued improperly

prosecution_strengths: Pattern evidence from multiple incidents creates a compelling narrative of persistent conduct

prosecution_strengths: Electronic harassment evidence (texts, calls, emails) is easily preserved and documented

Challenge whether the conduct meets the statutory definition of harassment versus protected speech or lawful activity
Argue that the communications had a legitimate purpose and were not intended to harass

Legitimate purpose — the contact was for lawful business or personal reasons

Misunderstanding — defendant did not intend to harass

prosecution_strengths: Mandatory reporter requirements ensure early detection

common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — defendant did not know the firearm was present

prosecution_strengths: Carrying in prohibited locations (schools, government buildings, bars) is separately penalized even with a valid CCW license

defense_opportunities: Wisconsin is an open-carry state — if the weapon was not concealed, the charge fails

prosecution_strengths: Ballistic evidence and bullet trajectory analysis can trace the discharge to a specific location and weapon

prosecution_strengths: Digital evidence (computer records, online account access, email logs) is extensively preserved and difficult to dispute

prosecution_strengths: Forensic accounting and financial records create a detailed paper trail of the diverted funds

defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent to permanently deprive — argue the defendant intended to repay the funds (though intent to return is generally not a defense to theft)

common_defenses: Authorization — defendant had permission to make the expenditures

prosecution_strengths: Document examination and handwriting analysis provide expert forensic evidence

prosecution_strengths: Documentary evidence (contracts, emails, financial records) establishes the scheme comprehensively

prosecution_strengths: Transaction records, surveillance footage at points of sale, and digital forensics provide clear evidence

prosecution_strengths: Financial forensics and banking records create a detailed trail of the laundered funds

No underlying criminal activity — the source of funds was legal
Insufficient evidence connecting the defendant to the laundering scheme

Misidentification — defendant was not the assailant

prosecution_strengths: Witness testimony from multiple observers is often available for public exposure incidents

Contest whether the conduct meets the statutory definition of 'publicly' indecent

prosecution_strengths: Officer testimony about observing the conduct is typically sufficient

Self-defense against excessive force by the officer
